rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to capture all 10 compounds and reveal the retention range and critical separations. The moderate gradient duration and temperature leave room to optimize selectivity and run time in subsequent injections.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin survives. Keep temperature and endpoints unchanged to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

Use a slightly shallower gradient to recover separation in the crowded middle region, and raise temperature to test whether selectivity improves for the critical cluster. Higher temperature may also offset the added gradient time by accelerating the last peak.

Increase temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test temperature-driven selectivity in the remaining critical pair. This may improve its resolution while keeping the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

Test the intermediate temperature: interpolation suggests 55 C could resolve the middle pair that is crowded at 50 C without causing the near-coelution seen at 60 C. The last peak should remain within the zero-time-penalty window.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly shallower gradient to explore whether another method can match it with a larger resolution margin. The last peak is expected to remain near the zero-time-penalty boundary.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a higher starting organic fraction to seek a faster method that retains full resolution. Keep temperature and gradient duration fixed to assess the effect on the two closest pairs.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to recover the separation lost with the higher starting organic fraction. This may bring both critical pairs above 1.5 while retaining a last-peak time below 8 minutes and matching the maximum CRF.

Reduce the gradient slope one more step to lift the remaining critical resolution above 1.5 while aiming to keep the last peak near 8 minutes. This tests whether the higher-starting-organic method can match the maximum CRF with a larger minimum separation.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a higher starting organic fraction combined with a shallower gradient to explore an alternative with greater resolution margin. The higher start may offset the longer gradient and keep the final peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so explore a lower-temperature selectivity regime with the shorter gradient. This tests whether cooling separates the crowded middle peaks while keeping the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

With CRF 1.000 already secured, explore a faster high-temperature, higher-starting-organic regime. The selectivity shift may move the previously crowded middle peaks past their elution-order crossover, though early-peak resolution will need checking.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve early-peak separation, and shorten the gradient to test whether the middle-pair crossover yields better selectivity at higher steepness. This explores a faster alternative while preserving the previously achieved maximum-CRF method.

This preserves the starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope of injection 5, so all peaks should elute under the same gradient and retain CRF 1.000. The lower endpoint shortens the programmed ramp without changing the gradient before the last observed peak.

Preserve the successful gradient slope while lowering the endpoint and ending the ramp at 8 minutes. Since the last peak previously eluted at 7.60 minutes, this should reproduce the maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Use a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9 to balance their critical separations. This should bring both pairs above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes, potentially matching maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 5.

Preserve injection 9’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while lowering the endpoint. The gradient reaches its endpoint at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the observed last peak, so this should retain CRF 1.000 and its resolution margin.

Preserve the successful gradient slope through the first nine peaks, then hold at 50% organic to test a lower-endpoint alternative. The key question is whether the final compound still elutes within the zero-time-penalty window while retaining full resolution.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 9 to further separate its earlier critical pair while checking that the later pair remains above 1.5. Injection 18 shows that a last-peak time above 8 minutes can still incur no time penalty, leaving room for this adjustment to match CRF 1.000.

Reduce the gradient slope from injection 10 to improve its limiting separation while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. This tests whether both critical pairs can exceed 1.5 with more resolution margin and still match the maximum CRF.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 20 to push its limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the other separations. This tests whether the higher-starting-organic method can match CRF 1.000 before the longer retention incurs a time penalty.

Slightly flatten injection 19’s gradient to test the resolution margin around this maximum-scoring method. The later critical pair should remain above 1.5, and the last peak is expected before the approximately 9-minute onset of the time penalty.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 5 to seek a faster maximum-scoring method. The later critical pair may improve, but the earlier pair’s small resolution margin makes this a useful boundary test.

Test a gradient slope between the maximum-scoring injections 19 and 22. Both critical separations are expected to remain above 1.5, with the last peak below 9 minutes, providing another method likely to match CRF 1.000.

Use a gradient slope between the maximum-scoring injections 19 and 24, with a lower endpoint reached after the expected last peak. This final method is expected to retain all 10 peaks, resolution above 1.5, and no time penalty, matching the already achieved maximum CRF of 1.000.
